\chapter{From the Seed Up --- Seed, Root, Trunk, Branch, Wood}
\label{ch:de-la-semilla}
\hlchaptermodality{291}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the seed, the root, the trunk, the branch and the wood in Spanish.}

Complete ES-C291-bosque: name all five from the ground upwards, seed to forest.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la semilla]{la semilla — where a seminar gets its name}

\label{lesson:ES-C291-semilla}



\begin{quote}
Before a new run: what was \emph{mel}? (Honey.) And what language gave Spanish \emph{tomate}? (Nahuatl.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la flor — what this one is left behind by.
  \item el trigo — a crop that is nothing but these.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{se-MI-lla}, stress in the middle. The \emph{ll} is the \emph{y} sound again, the same as in \emph{cebolla}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la semilla} — \textquotedblleft{}the seed.\textquotedblright{}

Behind it sits Latin \textbf{seminalia}, \textquotedblleft{}the things for sowing,\textquotedblright{} and behind that \textbf{semen}, which meant a seed long before it meant anything narrower.

The English family is unusually respectable. A \textbf{seminar} is a seed-bed, a place where ideas are started rather than finished. A \textbf{seminary} is a nursery for people. To \textbf{disseminate} is to scatter seed in every direction, which is what \emph{dis-} is doing there. And something \textbf{seminal} is the thing everything later grew out of.

Hear the \emph{-illa} on the end again. This is the second time it has turned up in two chapters' worth of words, and it will keep turning up — a small ending doing quiet work in words nobody thinks of as small any more.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One word, and the beginning of a shape.

The next few belong together: this is a tree taken from the ground upwards, and you are standing at the bottom of it. Learning words in a set like that is worth more than learning five unrelated ones, because the set itself is a hook.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la semilla}
  \item \emph{la semilla}, then \emph{seminar} — the seed and the seed-bed
  \item \emph{la semilla del trigo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{seminalia} mean? (Things for sowing.) What is a \emph{seminar}, taken apart? (A seed-bed.) And what does \emph{dis-} add to \emph{disseminate}? (Scattering in all directions.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la raíz]{la raíz — the word this book keeps using about words}

\label{lesson:ES-C291-raiz}



\begin{quote}
Two back: what was \emph{mel}? (Honey.) And what is a \emph{seminar}, taken apart? (A seed-bed.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la semilla — what this comes out of first.
  \item el árbol — what is standing on top of it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ra-ÍZ}, two beats, stress on the second. The written accent is doing real work: it splits \emph{a} and \emph{i} apart instead of letting them slide together. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la raíz} — \textquotedblleft{}the root.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{radix}, and this is the one word in the set you have already been using in English without noticing, because it is what we say about words themselves. When a lesson says a Spanish word and an English word share a root, \emph{radix} is the metaphor underneath.

A \textbf{radish} is a \emph{radix} that got eaten. A \textbf{radical} goes to the root of the matter, which is why the word means both \textquotedblleft{}fundamental\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}extreme\textquotedblright{} — it depends whether you approve. To \textbf{eradicate} is to pull up by the roots, \emph{e-} out plus \emph{radix}. And a square \textbf{root} in mathematics is a translation of the same Latin.

The accent on the \emph{í} is not decoration. Without it, \emph{ai} would slide into one sound; with it, the two vowels stay separate and the stress lands on the second.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two, and they are in the right order: the seed, then what comes out of it first.

You also have the etymology of the word \emph{root} itself, which is a small thing until you notice that half of what this approach does is claim two words share one. Now you can say that claim in Spanish.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la raíz}
  \item \emph{la semilla}, then \emph{la raíz} — in that order
  \item \emph{ra-íz}, two beats, and keep the vowels apart
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{radix}? (A root.) What does \emph{eradicate} say, taken apart? (To pull out by the roots.) And what is the accent on \emph{raíz} doing? (Keeping the two vowels in separate beats.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el tronco]{el tronco — a word that means \textquotedblleft{}cut short\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C291-tronco}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what was \emph{radix}? (A root.) And what did \emph{seminalia} mean? (Things for sowing.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la raíz — what holds this up.
  \item el árbol — the whole of which this is the middle.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{TRON-co}, stress on the first part. The \emph{c} before \emph{o} is the hard one, and the \emph{n} closes the first beat. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el tronco} — \textquotedblleft{}the trunk.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{truncus}, and its first meaning was not a tree at all. \emph{Truncus} meant lopped, maimed, cut short — a thing with its ends taken off. A tree stripped of branches is a \emph{truncus}, and the name stuck to the part that was left.

English took the whole family. A \textbf{trunk} is the same word. To \textbf{truncate} is to cut short deliberately. A \textbf{truncheon} is a stick that is a cut-off piece of something longer. Even the elephant's trunk and the traveller's trunk are the same word wandering off in two directions from one idea of a thick stump.

That first meaning explains something odd about \emph{tronco} in Spanish: it is used of a body as well as a tree, for the part left when you set aside the head and the limbs. It has never really stopped meaning \textquotedblleft{}what remains.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, going upward: \emph{la semilla}, \emph{la raíz}, \emph{el tronco}.

The set is doing the work of a story. You are not holding three separate items in mind, you are holding one tree, and the order of the words is the order of the thing itself.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el tronco}
  \item \emph{la semilla}, \emph{la raíz}, \emph{el tronco} — bottom to middle
  \item \emph{el tronco del árbol}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{truncus} mean first? (Lopped, cut short.) What does \emph{truncate} do? (Cuts something short.) And what are the first three of the set? (\emph{La semilla}, \emph{la raíz}, \emph{el tronco}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la rama]{la rama — what a ramification actually is}

\label{lesson:ES-C291-rama}



\begin{quote}
Quick pass: what did \emph{truncus} mean? (Lopped short.) What was \emph{radix}? (A root.) And what is \emph{la semilla}? (The seed.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el tronco — what these come out of.
  \item el árbol — the whole thing they belong to.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{RA-ma}, stress on the first part. The opening \emph{r} at the start of a word is rolled, not tapped. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la rama} — \textquotedblleft{}the branch.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{ramus}, and it has barely moved: drop the ending, soften nothing, and there it is.

English kept \emph{ramus} only in its abstract clothes, which makes the connection easy to miss. When a problem \textbf{ramifies}, it is growing branches. A \textbf{ramification} is one branch of a consequence. Both words are used almost entirely about arguments and lawsuits, and both are describing a tree.

This is a pattern worth naming. Spanish very often keeps a Latin word for the physical thing while English keeps it only for the metaphor. \emph{Rama} is a branch you can snap; \textbf{ramification} is a branch nobody can point at. Same word, and the two languages divided the labour between them.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and the tree is nearly whole: \emph{la semilla}, \emph{la raíz}, \emph{el tronco}, \emph{la rama}.

Four words, and not one of them needed a rule you did not already have. They are ordinary things with ordinary endings, and the only work you have done is hearing what was already inside them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la rama}
  \item \emph{la rama del árbol}
  \item \emph{la semilla}, \emph{la raíz}, \emph{el tronco}, \emph{la rama}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{ramus}? (A branch.) What is a \emph{ramification}, underneath? (A branch of a consequence.) And which four do you have so far? (\emph{La semilla}, \emph{la raíz}, \emph{el tronco}, \emph{la rama}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el bosque]{el bosque — the one in the set that is not Roman}

\label{lesson:ES-C291-bosque}



\begin{quote}
Before the last of the five: what was \emph{ramus}? (A branch.) What was \emph{truncus}? (Lopped short.) And what was \emph{radix}? (A root.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el árbol — one of these, many times over.
  \item la rama — the word before this one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{BOS-que}, stress on the first part. The \emph{qu} is a plain hard \emph{k} and the \emph{u} is silent, as it is in \emph{qué}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el bosque} — \textquotedblleft{}the wood,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the forest.\textquotedblright{}

Take this one apart and Latin does not answer. \emph{Bosque} is Germanic — from a root like \textbf{busk}, a thicket — and it walked into Spanish with the Visigoths, who ruled the peninsula for three centuries between Rome and the Arabic arrival.

Which means its English relative is a native one. A \textbf{bush} is the same word. A \textbf{bosky} wood is a thicketed one. To \textbf{ambush} is to lie in the bushes, \emph{in} the \emph{busk}, waiting. And a \textbf{bouquet} is French for a little wood, a small stand of stems, which is a fair description of what is in the vase.

Spanish is often described as Latin plus Arabic, and that is most of the truth, but there is a Germanic layer underneath. You have already met \emph{blanco}, which is Germanic too. \emph{Bosque} is that layer showing again.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \emph{la semilla}, \emph{la raíz}, \emph{el tronco}, \emph{la rama}, \emph{el bosque}.

Said in order they build one tree and then step back to show a thousand of them. Four came from Rome and the fifth from the north, so this short set has quietly handed you the three sources Spanish draws on — Latin, Arabic in the chapter before, and now Germanic.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el bosque}
  \item \emph{bosque}, then \emph{bush} — the same thicket twice
  \item all five — \emph{la semilla}, \emph{la raíz}, \emph{el tronco}, \emph{la rama}, \emph{el bosque}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \emph{bosque} come from? (Germanic, not Latin.) Which English words are its cousins? (\emph{Bush}, \emph{bosky}, \emph{ambush}.) And which other Germanic word do you already have? (\emph{Blanco}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
